subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: 13.5 Circuits with Resistors and Inductors (LR Circuits)
13.6 Circuits with Capacitors and Inductors (LC Circuits)

questions.q: A student is choosing a Gaussian surface in order to apply Gauss’s law. Which statement about Gaussian surfaces is correct?
options: A Gaussian surface is the physical surface of the object that carries the charge.
A Gaussian surface can be open, like a flat disk, as long as field lines cross it.
A Gaussian surface can be any closed surface, even one that passes through empty space.
A Gaussian surface must match the charges’ symmetry, or Gauss’s law fails.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a Gaussian surface must be a real boundary picks this. The surface is imaginary and is drawn through the point where the field is wanted, which is often in empty space away from the object.
A student who applies Gauss’s law to any surface the field crosses picks this. Gauss’s law relates flux to enclosed charge, and only a closed surface encloses anything; a disk encloses nothing.

A Gaussian surface is an imaginary, closed, three-dimensional surface. It can have any shape and can pass through empty space or through material, and Gauss’s law holds for every such surface. A shape that matches the symmetry is chosen only because it makes the flux integral easy to evaluate.
A student who confuses when Gauss’s law is useful with when it is true picks this. The law holds for every closed surface; a surface that matches the symmetry is needed only to calculate E from it.
questions.explain: A Gaussian surface is an imaginary, closed, three-dimensional surface. It can have any shape and can pass through empty space or through material, and Gauss’s law holds for every such surface. A shape that matches the symmetry is chosen only because it makes the flux integral easy to evaluate.

questions.q: For which of the following can Gauss’s law, with a suitably chosen Gaussian surface, be used to calculate the magnitude of the electric field at the stated point?
options: A very long, uniformly charged solid cylinder, at a point 3 cm from its axis
A uniformly charged solid cube, at a point 1 cm from the center of one of the cube’s faces
A uniformly charged rod 20 cm long, at a point 3 cm from the midpoint of the rod
A sphere with +Q on its upper half and −Q on its lower half, at a point far from it
optionWhy: A very long cylinder has cylindrical symmetry. On a coaxial Gaussian cylinder through the point, E is radial with one magnitude over the curved side and parallel to the end caps, so the flux is E(2πrℓ), whether the point is inside or outside the charged cylinder, and E follows from q_enc.

A student who thinks any Gaussian surface shaped like the charged object will work picks this. Over a cube-shaped surface around a charged cube, the field changes in size and direction from point to point, so E cannot be taken out of the flux integral.

A student who treats a rod of finite length like an infinite line picks this. Along a coaxial cylinder around a 20 cm rod the field has components along the rod and changes in size, so the curved side’s flux is not E(2πrℓ) and the end caps carry flux.

A student who takes zero net flux to mean zero field picks this: a concentric Gaussian sphere encloses zero net charge, which seems to give E = 0. Zero net flux means only that inward and outward flux cancel; this sphere’s field is not zero, and it varies in size and direction over the Gaussian sphere.
questions.explain: A very long cylinder has cylindrical symmetry. On a coaxial Gaussian cylinder through the point, E is radial with one magnitude over the curved side and parallel to the end caps, so the flux is E(2πrℓ), whether the point is inside or outside the charged cylinder, and E follows from q_enc.
questions.working: Only the very long cylinder has one of the three symmetries (cylindrical): a coaxial Gaussian cylinder through the point 3 cm from the axis has E radial and uniform over its curved side and zero flux through its ends, so E(2πrℓ) = q_enc/ε₀. The cube, the 20 cm rod and the sphere with oppositely charged halves give a field that varies in size and direction over any closed surface, so Gauss’s law gives the flux but not E.

questions.q: Gauss’s law is the first of Maxwell’s equations, the set of equations that together fully describe electromagnetism. Which statement about Gauss’s law is correct?
options: It holds for highly symmetric charge distributions and fails for others.
It gives the field of any charged object when the Gaussian surface matches its shape.
It is Coulomb’s law restated, so it holds for point charges but no others.
It holds for every closed surface, whatever charges lie inside or outside it.
optionWhy: A student who confuses when Gauss’s law is true with when it is useful picks this. The law holds for every distribution; only calculating E from it directly needs spherical, cylindrical or planar symmetry.

A student who thinks Gauss’s law yields E whenever the Gaussian surface copies the object’s shape picks this. The law always gives the net flux, but E can be taken out of the flux integral only with spherical, cylindrical or planar symmetry; over a cube-shaped surface around a charged cube, E varies in size and direction.

A student who sees Gauss’s law as Coulomb’s law rewritten for a point charge picks this. For a point charge the two give the same field, but Gauss’s law holds for any charge distribution; it is one of the equations that fully describe electromagnetism.

As one of Maxwell’s equations, Gauss’s law is a general law: the net flux through any closed surface equals q_enc/ε₀, for any arrangement of charges. Symmetry decides only whether the law can be used on its own to calculate E, and charges outside the surface add zero net flux.
questions.explain: As one of Maxwell’s equations, Gauss’s law is a general law: the net flux through any closed surface equals q_enc/ε₀, for any arrangement of charges. Symmetry decides only whether the law can be used on its own to calculate E, and charges outside the surface add zero net flux.

questions.q: A particle with charge +q is held at rest between the north and south poles of a large horseshoe magnet, where the magnetic field is strong. Which statement about the magnetic force on the particle is correct?
options: It is pulled toward the south pole, which acts like a negative charge.
There is no magnetic force on it, since it is not moving at all.
It is pushed along B⃗ by a force of size qB, as in an electric field.
It is pushed at right angles to B⃗, as magnetic forces act sideways.
optionWhy: A student who treats magnetic poles as electric charges picks this. The south pole is not a negative charge; a magnet exerts no magnetic force on a charge at rest.
A magnetic field exerts forces on moving charges, currents and magnetic materials. A charge at rest is none of these, so it feels no magnetic force, however strong the field.

A student who carries F⃗ = qE⃗ over to magnetic fields picks this. There is no magnetic force of the form qB along the field; a magnetic force on a moving charge is perpendicular to B⃗, and here the charge is not moving.
A student who thinks every charge in a magnetic field feels a magnetic force picks this. Magnetic forces on charges are indeed sideways, but only on moving charges; this charge is at rest.
questions.explain: A magnetic field exerts forces on moving charges, currents and magnetic materials. A charge at rest is none of these, so it feels no magnetic force, however strong the field.

questions.q: Which statement about the sources of magnetic fields is correct?
options: Every source is a dipole or a combination of dipoles; none is a single pole.
Each end of a bar magnet is a separate source, like a single point charge.
Only permanent magnets are sources; moving charges make electric fields only.
A charged object at rest is a source, with its charge acting as a magnetic pole.
optionWhy: Magnetic fields are produced by magnetic dipoles or combinations of dipoles, never by monopoles. A bar magnet, a compass needle and a current loop are all dipoles, each with both a north and a south pole.

A student who pictures each pole as a charge-like source picks this. The two poles of a magnet are not separate sources: the field lines loop through the magnet, and no isolated pole has ever been found.

A student who separates magnetism from electricity picks this. Moving charges do produce magnetic fields: magnetic dipoles result from the circular or rotational motion of charges, including electrons in magnets.
A student who treats poles as electric charges picks this. A charge at rest produces an electric field but no magnetic field; charge is not a magnetic pole.
questions.explain: Magnetic fields are produced by magnetic dipoles or combinations of dipoles, never by monopoles. A bar magnet, a compass needle and a current loop are all dipoles, each with both a north and a south pole.

questions.q: An iron rod and an aluminum rod of the same size are held in turn at the same place near a strong magnet. The iron rod is pulled strongly toward the magnet; no effect on the aluminum rod can be seen. Which explanation is correct?
options: Iron is denser than aluminum, so there is more metal for the magnet to pull on.
Aluminum is not a magnetic material, so the field exerts no force on it.
Iron's atomic dipoles align strongly with the field; aluminum's align only weakly.
The field creates dipoles in both rods, but it creates far more of them in the iron.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a magnet pulls harder on more massive objects picks this. The difference is in the type of material: a much heavier block of aluminum would still barely respond.
A student who thinks 'non-magnetic' means 'unaffected' picks this. Aluminum is weakly attracted (paramagnetic); the force exists but is too small to see with an ordinary magnet.

A material's composition sets its magnetic behavior. Iron is ferromagnetic: its dipoles align strongly with an external field, so it is strongly attracted. Aluminum is paramagnetic: its dipoles align only weakly, so the attraction is too small to notice.

A student who thinks an external field creates the dipoles in a material picks this. The atoms of both metals already have dipoles; the field only aligns them, strongly in iron and weakly in aluminum.
questions.explain: A material's composition sets its magnetic behavior. Iron is ferromagnetic: its dipoles align strongly with an external field, so it is strongly attracted. Aluminum is paramagnetic: its dipoles align only weakly, so the attraction is too small to notice.

questions.q: The figure shows a cross section through the middle part of a long solenoid carrying a steady current, and three points, 1, 2 and 3. B₁, B₂ and B₃ are the magnitudes of the magnetic field at these points. Which ranking is correct?
options: B₂ > B₁ > B₃
B₁ = B₂ > B₃
B₁ > B₂ > B₃
B₁ = B₂ = B₃
optionWhy: A student who pictures the field inside as the field near a single wire, strongest close to the windings, picks this. Inside a long solenoid the field is uniform, the same near the windings as on the axis.
A long solenoid’s field is uniform inside, so it is the same on the axis (point 1) as near the windings (point 2), and it is negligible outside (point 3).
A student who expects the field to be strongest on the axis picks this. For a long solenoid the field is the same everywhere inside, on the axis or close to the windings.
A student who thinks the field just outside is as strong as the field inside picks this. For a long solenoid the field outside is negligible, so B₃ is much smaller than B₁ and B₂.
questions.explain: A long solenoid’s field is uniform inside, so it is the same on the axis (point 1) as near the windings (point 2), and it is negligible outside (point 3).
questions.working: A long solenoid has a uniform field inside and a negligible field outside. Points 1 (on the axis) and 2 (inside, near the windings) are both inside: B₁ = B₂ = μ₀nI. Point 3 is outside: B₃ ≈ 0. So B₁ = B₂ > B₃.

figure.alt: Cross section through the middle part of a long solenoid: a top row of wire cross sections drawn as ⊗ (current into the page) and a bottom row drawn as ⊙ (current out of the page). Three dots lie on a vertical line through the middle: point 1 on the solenoid’s axis, midway between the rows; point 2 inside the solenoid, just below the top row of windings; point 3 outside the solenoid, just above the top row. A caption reads long solenoid (middle section shown).

questions.q: To derive the field inside a long solenoid, a rectangular Amperian loop is drawn with one long side inside the solenoid, parallel to its axis, and the opposite long side outside it; the two short sides cross the windings. Which statement about the contributions of the four sides to ∮B⃗ · dℓ⃗ is correct?
options: Both long sides contribute equally, as the field outside matches the field inside.
All four sides contribute, as each lies at least partly in the solenoid’s field.
Only the long side inside contributes, as B⃗ is parallel to it there.
Only the short sides contribute, as B⃗ is perpendicular to them inside.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the field outside a long solenoid is as strong as the field inside picks this. For a long solenoid the field outside is negligible, so the outside side contributes nothing.

A student who counts every side that lies in a field picks this. B⃗ · dℓ⃗ keeps only the component of B⃗ along the path, and inside the solenoid B⃗ is perpendicular to the short sides, so they add nothing.

Inside the solenoid the field is uniform and parallel to the axis, so along the inside long side B⃗ · dℓ⃗ = B dℓ and that side contributes Bℓ. Outside, the field is negligible. On the short sides, B⃗ is perpendicular to dℓ⃗ inside the solenoid and negligible outside, so they contribute nothing.

A student who mixes up the dot and cross products picks this. B⃗ · dℓ⃗ = B dℓ cos θ is zero where B⃗ is perpendicular to the path and largest where it is parallel, which is along the inside long side.
questions.explain: Inside the solenoid the field is uniform and parallel to the axis, so along the inside long side B⃗ · dℓ⃗ = B dℓ and that side contributes Bℓ. Outside, the field is negligible. On the short sides, B⃗ is perpendicular to dℓ⃗ inside the solenoid and negligible outside, so they contribute nothing.

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor is being charged, with a steady current in the wires connected to its plates. Which statement about the region between the plates is correct?
options: There is no magnetic field, because no charges move across the gap between the two plates.
The increasing electric field between the plates produces a magnetic field that circles that region.
A magnetic field is present, produced by the electric field and lasting while that field remains.
A magnetic field is present, produced by charges carried across the gap from plate to plate.
optionWhy: A student who thinks only moving charges produce magnetic fields picks this. It is true that no charge crosses the gap, but a changing electric field also produces a magnetic field.

While the capacitor charges, the electric field between the plates increases. By Maxwell’s addition to Ampère’s law, a changing electric field produces a magnetic field, so a magnetic field circles the region between the plates although no charge crosses the gap.

A student who thinks any electric field produces a magnetic field picks this. It is the change in the electric field that produces the magnetic field; once charging stops and the field is steady, this source is gone.

A student who thinks the current passes through the capacitor picks this. No charge crosses the insulating gap; charge builds up on the plates, and the magnetic field between them is produced by the changing electric field.
questions.explain: While the capacitor charges, the electric field between the plates increases. By Maxwell’s addition to Ampère’s law, a changing electric field produces a magnetic field, so a magnetic field circles the region between the plates although no charge crosses the gap.

questions.q: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a sensitive ammeter, held at rest inside the coil, and then pulled back out. Which describes the emf induced in the coil while the magnet is at rest, and the direction of the emf while the magnet is pulled out compared with while it was pushed in?
options: Nonzero while at rest; opposite in direction while it is pulled out
Zero while at rest; the same direction as before while it is pulled out
Largest while at rest; the same direction as before while it is pulled out
Zero while at rest; opposite in direction while it is pulled out
optionWhy: A student who thinks an emf is induced whenever a field passes through the coil picks this. With the magnet at rest the flux is steady, so dΦ_B/dt = 0 and there is no emf, however strong the field.

A student who thinks the induced field always opposes the magnet's field predicts the same direction both times. The induced field opposes the change: it opposes the magnet's field while the flux increases, but points along it while the flux decreases, so the emf reverses.

A student who takes the emf to follow the flux itself picks this: the flux is largest with the magnet inside and keeps the same direction throughout. The emf depends on the rate of change of flux, which is zero while the magnet is at rest and changes sign when the flux starts to decrease.

An emf is induced only while the flux through the coil changes. At rest, the flux is large but steady, so the emf is zero. Pushing the magnet in increases the flux; pulling it out decreases it, so by Lenz's law the induced emf, and the current, reverse.
questions.explain: An emf is induced only while the flux through the coil changes. At rest, the flux is large but steady, so the emf is zero. Pushing the magnet in increases the flux; pulling it out decreases it, so by Lenz's law the induced emf, and the current, reverse.

questions.q: An electron is held at rest at a point outside a long solenoid, where the solenoid's magnetic field is negligible. The current in the solenoid begins to increase, and the electron is released. Which describes the force on the electron just after it is released?
options: An electric force directed along a radius, toward the solenoid's axis
An electric force tangent to a circle around the solenoid's axis
A magnetic force, as the flux through its circle around the axis changes
No force, as the magnetic field is negligible where the electron is
optionWhy: A student who pictures the induced field like the field of a charged wire picks this. The induced field has no charges to start or end on; around a solenoid its field lines are circles, so the force is tangential.

The increasing flux inside the solenoid induces an electric field outside it, whose field lines are circles centered on the axis. The electron at rest feels the electric force −eE⃗ of this field, tangent to such a circle, even though B is negligible where it is.

A student who calls the force magnetic because the cause is a changing magnetic flux picks this. The magnetic force q(v⃗ × B⃗) on a charge at rest is zero; the force is exerted by the induced electric field.
A student who thinks induced effects occur only where B is nonzero picks this. The electron lies on a circle enclosing changing flux, so the induced electric field at its position is not zero.
questions.explain: The increasing flux inside the solenoid induces an electric field outside it, whose field lines are circles centered on the axis. The electron at rest feels the electric force −eE⃗ of this field, tangent to such a circle, even though B is negligible where it is.

questions.q: Maxwell's equations predict electromagnetic waves. Which statement about electromagnetic waves and a vacuum (free space) agrees with this prediction?
options: In a vacuum those of higher frequency travel faster than the others.
They cannot cross a vacuum, as any wave needs a medium to carry it.
In a vacuum their speed depends on the speed of the source emitting them.
In a vacuum all of them travel at the same speed, whatever their frequency.
optionWhy: A student who thinks more energetic waves move faster picks this. The speed in free space is fixed by ε_0 and μ_0 alone; a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength, not a higher speed.

A student who generalizes from sound picks this. An electromagnetic wave consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, which exist in empty space; light crosses the vacuum between the Sun and Earth.
A student who adds the source's speed to the wave's, as for objects thrown from a moving vehicle, picks this. The speed in free space is the constant c, whatever the motion of the source.

Maxwell's equations show that the electric and magnetic fields obey wave equations with one wave speed in free space, c = 1/√(ε_0 μ_0) = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, which depends on no property of the wave. Different frequencies have different wavelengths, not different speeds.
questions.explain: Maxwell's equations show that the electric and magnetic fields obey wave equations with one wave speed in free space, c = 1/√(ε_0 μ_0) = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, which depends on no property of the wave. Different frequencies have different wavelengths, not different speeds.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the effect of an inductor on the current in the circuit that contains it?
options: It opposes the current itself, reducing even a steady current.
It opposes increases in its current but lets a decrease happen freely.
It passes current only until charge builds up on its turns, then stops it.
It opposes any change in its current, increase or decrease.
optionWhy: A student who thinks an inductor acts like a resistor picks this. With a steady current, dI/dt = 0 and an ideal inductor has no effect; it opposes only changes.
A student who links an inductor only to delaying a rising current picks this. When the current decreases, the induced emf acts to keep it going, opposing the decrease.

A student who thinks an inductor stores charge as a capacitor does expects the current to stop once the inductor is charged. An inductor stores no net charge; once its current is steady, an ideal inductor behaves as a wire.
Inductance is the tendency to oppose a change in current. The induced emf, −L dI/dt, opposes increases and decreases alike, and it is zero when the current is steady.
questions.explain: Inductance is the tendency to oppose a change in current. The induced emf, −L dI/dt, opposes increases and decreases alike, and it is zero when the current is steady.

questions.q: In analyzing a circuit, which of the following elements is modeled as having significant inductance?
options: A tightly wound solenoid
A long straight wire
A charged capacitor
A high-value resistor
optionWhy: A solenoid links the field of its own current through many turns, so it has significant inductance; that is what makes it an inductor. Straight wires are modeled as having zero inductance, and capacitors and resistors are modeled without inductance.

A student who thinks inductance grows with the length of wire, as resistance does, picks this. Straight wires are typically modeled as having zero inductance; it is coiling the wire that gives significant inductance.

A student who thinks an inductor works by storing charge, as a capacitor does, takes a charged capacitor to be an inductor and picks this. A capacitor stores energy in an electric field and is modeled with capacitance, not inductance; an inductor stores no net charge.
A student who thinks inductance is a kind of resistance picks this. A resistor opposes the current itself and dissipates energy; it is modeled as having no inductance.
questions.explain: A solenoid links the field of its own current through many turns, so it has significant inductance; that is what makes it an inductor. Straight wires are modeled as having zero inductance, and capacitors and resistors are modeled without inductance.

questions.q: An ideal inductor that carries a current is connected across a resistor, with no battery in the circuit, and its current decreases to zero. Which statement about energy during this process is correct?
options: The fall in the inductor's stored energy equals the energy the resistor dissipates.
The inductor itself turns its stored energy into thermal energy as it opposes the change.
The inductor's stored energy disappears once the current and its magnetic field reach zero.
The resistor dissipates more energy than was stored, as the inductor's emf adds more.
optionWhy: Energy is conserved. The ideal inductor dissipates nothing; as its current falls, the energy stored in its magnetic field is transferred to the resistor, which dissipates exactly that amount as thermal energy.
A student who thinks opposing a change means dissipating energy, as a resistor does, picks this. An ideal inductor has no resistance and dissipates nothing; the resistor dissipates the energy.
A student who thinks the energy vanishes with the field picks this. Energy is conserved: it is transferred to the resistor as the current decreases.
A student who treats every emf as an energy source picks this. With no battery, the only energy available is the (1/2)LI² stored at the start; the inductor's emf only transfers it.
questions.explain: Energy is conserved. The ideal inductor dissipates nothing; as its current falls, the energy stored in its magnetic field is transferred to the resistor, which dissipates exactly that amount as thermal energy.

questions.q: A battery, a switch and a resistor R₁ are connected in series with a parallel combination of an ideal inductor and a resistor R₂. The switch has been closed for a long time and is then opened. Which statement correctly describes what happens to the energy stored in the inductor after the switch is opened?
options: It stays in the inductor's magnetic field, since the battery is no longer connected.
It decreases as the current in the inductor and R₂ decreases, and R₂ dissipates it.
It is turned into thermal energy in the inductor, which opposes the change in current.
It is gone at the instant the switch opens, because every current stops at that instant.
optionWhy: A student who treats the inductor like a charged capacitor, which keeps its energy when it is isolated, picks this. An inductor stores energy only while it carries a current; its current continues through R₂ and decreases, and R₂ dissipates the energy.

Just before the switch opens, the inductor acts as a wire and carries a steady current, storing (1/2)LI². Its current cannot stop instantly, so after the switch opens it continues around the loop formed by the inductor and R₂ and decreases exponentially. As the current decreases, the stored energy (1/2)LI² decreases, and R₂ dissipates it as thermal energy. R₁ is in the branch that the open switch disconnects, so it carries no current.

A student who thinks the inductor's opposition to the change works like a resistor's opposition to the current picks this. An ideal inductor has no resistance and dissipates nothing: it returns its stored energy to the circuit, and R₂ dissipates it.

A student who thinks the battery must drive every current picks this. The inductor's current cannot change instantaneously; it continues through R₂ and decreases over a time set by τ = L/R₂, so the energy is transferred to R₂ gradually.
questions.explain: Just before the switch opens, the inductor acts as a wire and carries a steady current, storing (1/2)LI². Its current cannot stop instantly, so after the switch opens it continues around the loop formed by the inductor and R₂ and decreases exponentially. As the current decreases, the stored energy (1/2)LI² decreases, and R₂ dissipates it as thermal energy. R₁ is in the branch that the open switch disconnects, so it carries no current.

questions.q: A series circuit contains a battery, a resistor, an ideal inductor and a switch. What does the time constant τ of the circuit describe?
options: How far the inductor lowers the steady current below the value set by the resistor
How rapidly the current approaches its final value after the switch is closed
How long the inductor's magnetic field lasts once its current stops changing
How long the current takes to reach its final value and then stop changing
optionWhy: A student who thinks an inductor opposes the current itself, even when it is steady, picks this. In the steady state dI/dt = 0 and an ideal inductor behaves as a wire, so it does not lower the steady current, ε/R.

τ = L/R_eq sets the time scale of the exponential change: after one τ the current has made about 63 percent of its change, and after a time much greater than τ it is effectively steady. The smaller τ is, the sooner the circuit approaches its steady state.

A student who thinks an inductor has a magnetic field only while its current changes picks this. A steady current keeps a steady field in the inductor for as long as it flows; τ describes how the current changes, not how long the field lasts.

A student who thinks τ is the time to reach the steady state picks this. After one τ the current has made only about 63 percent of its change; it approaches its final value more and more slowly and is effectively steady only after a time much greater than τ.
questions.explain: τ = L/R_eq sets the time scale of the exponential change: after one τ the current has made about 63 percent of its change, and after a time much greater than τ it is effectively steady. The smaller τ is, the sooner the circuit approaches its steady state.

questions.q: A series circuit contains an ideal battery of emf ε, a resistor, an ideal inductor and an open switch. The switch is closed at t = 0. Which statement correctly describes the emf induced in the inductor just after the switch is closed?
options: Its magnitude is ε, and it is directed opposite to the battery's emf around the loop.
Its magnitude is ε, and it acts in the same direction as the battery's emf around the loop.
It is zero, because at that instant there is not yet any current in the inductor.
Its magnitude is less than ε, because the resistor takes part of the battery's potential difference.
optionWhy: Just after closing, the current is still zero, so the potential difference across the resistor, IR, is zero, and the loop rule puts the whole of ε across the inductor. The induced emf opposes the increase in current, so it is directed opposite to the battery's emf: equal in magnitude, opposite in direction.

A student who thinks the induced emf helps the battery drive the growing current picks this. By Lenz's law the induced emf opposes the change, here an increase in current, so it acts against the battery's emf.
A student who thinks an inductor's emf depends on its current picks this. The emf depends on dI/dt, which is largest, ε/L, at the instant the switch closes, even though the current itself is zero.

A student who thinks the resistor always takes its share of the battery's potential difference picks this. With zero current, the resistor's potential difference, IR, is zero, so the inductor's emf has the full magnitude ε.
questions.explain: Just after closing, the current is still zero, so the potential difference across the resistor, IR, is zero, and the loop rule puts the whole of ε across the inductor. The induced emf opposes the increase in current, so it is directed opposite to the battery's emf: equal in magnitude, opposite in direction.

questions.q: A charged capacitor is connected across an ideal inductor at t = 0, with no resistance in the circuit. Which describes the charge on the capacitor after t = 0?
options: It decreases exponentially to zero and then stays zero, as it does in an RC circuit.
It oscillates, reversing its polarity each half cycle, with a constant amplitude.
It oscillates with an amplitude that shrinks as the current uses up energy flowing around.
It falls to zero and then returns to its first value, keeping the same polarity throughout.
optionWhy: A student who pictures every capacitor discharge as an RC discharge picks this. The inductor keeps the current going when q reaches zero, so the capacitor recharges with the opposite polarity.

The loop rule gives d²q/dt² = −q/(LC), the equation of simple harmonic motion, so q(t) = Q₀ cos(ωt): it passes through zero, reverses sign and returns, and with no resistance to dissipate energy the amplitude stays Q₀.

A student who thinks current uses up energy as it flows picks this. With no resistance nothing dissipates energy, so the energy passes back and forth between capacitor and inductor and the amplitude stays constant.

A student who pictures the charge flowing out of the capacitor and back in picks this. When q reaches zero the current is at its maximum and carries on, charging the capacitor with the opposite polarity.
questions.explain: The loop rule gives d²q/dt² = −q/(LC), the equation of simple harmonic motion, so q(t) = Q₀ cos(ωt): it passes through zero, reverses sign and returns, and with no resistance to dissipate energy the amplitude stays Q₀.

questions.q: In an ideal LC circuit, at the instant when the current is at its maximum, which statement about the energy stored in the circuit is correct?
options: Half of it is in the inductor and half is in the capacitor then.
All of it is in the inductor, since the capacitor is uncharged then.
Most of it is in the capacitor, since its charge is greatest then.
None of it is in the inductor, since its current is not changing then.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the energy is shared equally at maximum current picks this. Equal sharing happens only when q = Q₀/√2; at maximum current the charge is zero.
The current is greatest at the instant the capacitor's charge passes through zero, so U_C = q²/(2C) = 0 and all of the circuit's constant total energy is in the inductor, (1/2)LI_max².
A student who thinks the current is greatest when the charge is greatest picks this. At maximum current the charge on the capacitor is zero, so the capacitor stores no energy.

A student who thinks an inductor stores energy only while its current changes picks this. At maximum current dI/dt = 0, so the inductor's emf is zero, but its stored energy (1/2)LI² is at its greatest.
